bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- Largest private sector dairy in India, with scale economies management says allow investment in production and distribution infrastructure 'affordable only by bigger Companies like us'
- Backward-integrated procurement: milk sourced daily from over 500,000 farmers, with over 13,226+ milk collection centre points and Active Bulk Coolers at more than 1,553 locations chilling milk within two hours
- Direct farmer relationship — payments made every 10 days directly into farmer bank accounts on Fat and SNF test results, supported by a dedicated database, plus artificial insemination and cattle-care services that improve yield and genetics
- Dense last-mile retail network: 4,200+ HAP daily outlets, 229+ ibaco outlets and 169+ HAP daily Village Hub stores as of 31st March 2026
- Multi-brand portfolio spanning fresh dairy (Arokya, Hatsun, Milky Moo), ice cream (Arun, ibaco), confectionery (Havia, Hanobar, Dako), beverages (Aniva) and cattle feed (Santosa)
- Brand trust built on quality control — Arokya milk undergoes 45 quality checks daily, well beyond the 32 mandatory tests prescribed by FSSAI; Arokya has over 30 years of presence since 1995
- Geographically distributed manufacturing: 22 plants across Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka, Maharashtra and Odisha, enabling efficient procurement and distribution
- Credit quality: CRISIL upgraded the long-term rating to CRISIL AA/Stable on 14th January 2026 from CRISIL AA-/Stable
- SAP ERP implementation supporting centralised online MIS control of operations across all units
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- High feed costs and cattle feed shortages — Rising input costs and shortages of cattle feed impact production levels and increase operational expenses for farmers, with feed costs accounting for over 50% of production costs and squeezing farmer margins. The shortage is linked to supply chain disruptions and increased demand, and makes it harder for dairy farmers to keep milk production consistent — a direct threat to the raw-milk supply base Hatsun procures from.
- Cold chain inefficiencies and spoilage — A severe lack of chilling centres and cold storage in rural areas causes spoilage before processing; frequent power outages disrupt refrigeration, inadequate refrigerated transport causes temperature fluctuations in transit, and improper handling during loading, unloading and last-mile delivery causes substantial product spoilage. Many operations still rely on manual logs rather than automated IoT-based monitoring, so deviations are detected too late.
- Low per-animal productivity in the Indian herd — Average yields are roughly half the global average, due to small-scale traditional practices, poor nutrition, limited genetic improvement, costly and scarce fodder, declining grazing land, inadequate veterinary services and heat stress. A fragmented structure limits adoption of modern technology and scientific breeding, and low output limits farmer income, perpetuating the cycle — constraining the volume of quality milk available for procurement.
- Livestock disease outbreaks and zoonotic threats — Nipah Virus, Lumpy Skin Disease and Bovine Brucellosis are flagged as major threats to the dairy industry. Lingering effects of previous outbreaks combined with a fodder crisis have challenged industry growth, and structural issues such as lack of traceability for stray cattle make outbreaks difficult to prevent despite vaccination efforts; heightened public health warnings on raw unpasteurised milk also affect category perception.
- Seasonality of milk production and price volatility — Production peaks in the cooler flush season (September-February) and drops in the lean season (March-August), affecting production costs and availability. Processors manage supply by converting surplus flush-season milk into Skimmed Milk Powder to meet lean-season demand, which causes price volatility and supply imbalances — and exposes inventory positions across the year.
- Competitive and market-price pressure, including from global dairy entrants — Fluctuating market prices and the absence of a minimum support price make dairy farming less viable for small farmers. The entry of global dairy giants with aggressive pricing and economies of scale is a threat to local producers, and potential trade deals with countries such as the EU could restrict India's ability to control dairy exports and protect the domestic market. Separately, the shift to organised dairy is itself increasing competition among organised players.
- Climate change and weather volatility — Rising temperatures and erratic rainfall patterns can disrupt fodder production, increase feed costs and reduce milk yield. Management also names fluctuating weather conditions among the 'unforeseen external negativities' the workforce must help mitigate, and the BRSR identifies GHG emissions as a material risk on the basis that emissions will rise as manufacturing capacity grows with production demand.
- Infrastructure, logistics and consumer willingness-to-pay — Inadequate infrastructure including cold storage facilities and transportation networks can lead to milk spoilage and inefficient distribution, and lack of access to technology and information hinders adoption of efficient dairy farming practices. In addition, a segment of the population may not prioritise milk quality, limiting willingness to pay for higher-quality products — a constraint on premiumisation.

business.body: HAP manufactures and markets dairy products, especially milk and milk products such as curd, ghee, paneer and SMP, along with ice creams. outlook.title: Growth verticals / optionality

outlook.body:
- Sustain profitability by expanding geographical area, adopting new technologies, launching new products, strengthening quick commerce and online marketing, and making capital investments
- Enter new markets by expanding geographical areas, launching new product ranges, adopting new technologies and using alternative market channels such as online marketing
- Secure consistent year-round availability and procurement of quality milk by improving per-animal yield through scientific methods, genetic improvement, scientific feeding and managed animal husbandry practices, and by educating farmers and supplying good quality feed
- Broaden the all-India footprint through the Milky Moo acquisition (shareholding of Milk Mantra Dairy Private Limited), strengthening presence in the eastern markets and enhancing procurement and distribution capabilities in key regions
- Deepen the position in branded value-added dairy — curd, paneer, buttermilk and yoghurt-based items — where consumer demand is rising
- Expand last-mile retail through the HAP daily outlet network, now 4,200+ outlets, extending beyond the traditional South Indian base into Maharashtra, Kerala, Odisha, Goa, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, West Bengal, Jharkhand, Gujarat, Bihar and the Andaman & Nicobar Islands
- Grow the Arun Icecreams portfolio through continued innovation, new formats and flavours across impulse and take-home categories, and sports/brand marketing partnerships such as the Indian Super League
- Take Arun Icecreams international, into markets including the USA, Abu Dhabi and Oman
- Leverage economies of scale and the ability to adopt new technologies requiring large investment in production and distribution infrastructure, which management says is affordable only by bigger companies
- Use SAP ERP and continuously upgraded IT infrastructure for centralised online MIS control across all units, increasing bandwidth and reducing operational costs
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: Hatsun Agro's FY26 expansion was driven by footprint, procurement infrastructure and retail build-out rather than a stated rupee capex programme. Procurement capacity was extended through Active Bulk Coolers now present at more than 1,553 locations and over 13,226+ milk collection centre points serving over 5 lakh farmers, supported by processing and packaging plants strategically located across Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka, Maharashtra and Odisha. The Company invested in advanced infrastructure including cold storage facilities established in multiple states, and states it continues to expand production capacity to meet growing consumer demand. Inorganic expansion came through the acquisition of the Milky Moo brand via the shareholding of Milk Mantra Dairy Private Limited, adding processing facilities, a farmer network and a value-added product portfolio in the eastern markets; Milk Mantra Dairy Private Limited was subsequently amalgamated into Hatsun Agro Product Limited with an appointed date of 1st April 2025, sanctioned by the NCLT Cuttack Bench by order dated 10th March 2026. Retail expansion took the HAP daily network to 4,200+ outlets, extending beyond the traditional Tamil Nadu, Pondicherry, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana base into Maharashtra, Kerala, Odisha, Goa, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, West Bengal, Jharkhand, Gujarat, Bihar and the Andaman & Nicobar Islands; HAP daily also introduced Village Hubs taking reach deeper into rural markets, growing to over 169+ stores as of 31st March. On the ice cream side, a strong focus on expansion led to the opening of 54 IPlus outlets so far, while ibaco operated over 229 outlets as of 31st March. International expansion is on the horizon, with Arun Icecreams entering new markets including the USA, Abu Dhabi and Oman, and a plan to launch 23 new SKUs in April 2026. The Company operates 22 plants and 3 offices in India plus one office in the USA (New Jersey), serving 27 states and union territories and 8 countries. Green capital expenditure on projects for pollution control, employee and community safety, climate change and converting solar energy into electricity was reported in the BRSR at ₹16.62 Crores for FY 2025-26 against ₹1.92 Crores in FY 2024-25.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Indian real GDP growth placed at 7.4 per cent in the First Advance Estimates for FY26, driven by domestic demand, with private consumption and capital formation supporting expansion; the FY27 outlook is shaped by these domestic strengths alongside evolving external conditions
- The dairy processing sector in India has a favourable outlook driven by rising disposable incomes, changing consumption patterns and increasing demand for healthy food supplements
- Structural shift from loose to branded, packaged and high-protein dairy, accelerating formalisation of the sector and increasing competition among organised players
- Urbanisation — India expected to have nearly 600 million urban residents by 2030, with urban households preferring branded and packaged milk, organised retail and e-commerce, and hygiene/quality/convenience
- Rising protein awareness, with ICMR recommending 0.83 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight, driving demand for protein-enriched milk, high-protein yogurt and lassi, and functional dairy beverages
- Branded dairy products growing 4-5 times faster than liquid milk in India, driven by innovation, convenience and higher margins, and linked to expansion of food service chains, QSRs and home consumption in Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities
- Quick commerce redefining dairy accessibility with 10-15 minute delivery, increasing demand for premium and branded dairy, expanding consumption into Tier-2 cities and encouraging impulse purchases
- India's ice cream market estimated at approximately USD 3.07 billion in 2026, projected to reach USD 5.39 billion by 2032 at a CAGR of around 9.84%, with volume growing at around 8.22% CAGR; impulse ice cream around 60.59% of 2026 market revenue and plant-based the fastest-growing category at around 14.19% volume CAGR
- Government support strengthening dairy infrastructure and productivity — NPDD, AHIDF, Rashtriya Gokul Mission and LHDC, plus the Kisan Credit Card ceiling raised to ₹5 lakh for agriculture and allied activities including dairy
- Union Budget 2026-27 raised the animal husbandry allocation to ₹6,153.46 Crores, a 16% increase over FY 2025-26 (₹5,302.83 Crores), with ₹1,055 Crores for NPDD, ₹2,010 Crores for LHDC, ₹800 Crores for Rashtriya Gokul Mission and ₹465 Crores for AHIDF
- Milk production growing at an accelerated 5%-6.5% pace, with high-pedigree cows expected to drive volume, while tighter regulatory standards and operational costs drive consolidation favouring organised, large-scale dairy processors
- Product-formulation trends towards lactose-free milk, probiotic yogurts, protein-fortified drinks, D2C subscription models, IoT/AI-enabled dairy-tech, and sustainable packaging
outlook.title: Demand & outlook drivers

deepdive.thesis: Hatsun is on track to hit ₹10,000 Cr revenue run rate in FY26, driven by volume growth and proprietary distribution, but faces near-term margin pressure from 8-10% milk procurement hikes and 30-40% packaging cost inflation due to geopolitical supply chain disruptions.

sk.overview: India is the world's largest milk producer, contributing ~26% of global milk production in CY25, and the Indian dairy market is stated at INR 12.0T in FY26 within a packaged food market of INR 15.8T and an F&B market of INR 74.0T. Milk and value-added dairy products (VADP) together account for ~76% of the packaged food market, with liquid milk at INR 5.9T and VADP at INR 6.1T in FY26; VADP is stated to represent ~51-52% of the dairy market and to grow faster than milk (12.4% vs 7.8% CAGR FY26-31). currentContext.expansion: Hatsun Agro's FY26 expansion was driven by footprint, procurement infrastructure and retail build-out rather than a stated rupee capex programme. Procurement capacity was extended through Active Bulk Coolers now present at more than 1,553 locations and over 13,226+ milk collection centre points serving over 5 lakh farmers, supported by processing and packaging plants strategically located across Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka, Maharashtra and Odisha. The Company invested in advanced infrastructure including cold storage facilities established in multiple states, and states it continues to expand production capacity to meet growing consumer demand. Inorganic expansion came through the acquisition of the Milky Moo brand via the shareholding of Milk Mantra Dairy Private Limited, adding processing facilities, a farmer network and a value-added product portfolio in the eastern markets; Milk Mantra Dairy Private Limited was subsequently amalgamated into Hatsun Agro Product Limited with an appointed date of 1st April 2025, sanctioned by the NCLT Cuttack Bench by order dated 10th March 2026. Retail expansion took the HAP daily network to 4,200+ outlets, extending beyond the traditional Tamil Nadu, Pondicherry, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana base into Maharashtra, Kerala, Odisha, Goa, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, West Bengal, Jharkhand, Gujarat, Bihar and the Andaman & Nicobar Islands; HAP daily also introduced Village Hubs taking reach deeper into rural markets, growing to over 169+ stores as of 31st March. On the ice cream side, a strong focus on expansion led to the opening of 54 IPlus outlets so far, while ibaco operated over 229 outlets as of 31st March. International expansion is on the horizon, with Arun Icecreams entering new markets including the USA, Abu Dhabi and Oman, and a plan to launch 23 new SKUs in April 2026. The Company operates 22 plants and 3 offices in India plus one office in the USA (New Jersey), serving 27 states and union territories and 8 countries. Green capital expenditure on projects for pollution control, employee and community safety, climate change and converting solar energy into electricity was reported in the BRSR at ₹16.62 Crores for FY 2025-26 against ₹1.92 Crores in FY 2024-25.

risks.risk: High feed costs and cattle feed shortages
risks.note: Rising input costs and shortages of cattle feed impact production levels and increase operational expenses for farmers, with feed costs accounting for over 50% of production costs and squeezing farmer margins. The shortage is linked to supply chain disruptions and increased demand, and makes it harder for dairy farmers to keep milk production consistent — a direct threat to the raw-milk supply base Hatsun procures from.

A severe lack of chilling centres and cold storage in rural areas causes spoilage before processing; frequent power outages disrupt refrigeration, inadequate refrigerated transport causes temperature fluctuations in transit, and improper handling during loading, unloading and last-mile delivery causes substantial product spoilage. Many operations still rely on manual logs rather than automated IoT-based monitoring, so deviations are detected too late.

risks.risk: Low per-animal productivity in the Indian herd
risks.note: Average yields are roughly half the global average, due to small-scale traditional practices, poor nutrition, limited genetic improvement, costly and scarce fodder, declining grazing land, inadequate veterinary services and heat stress. A fragmented structure limits adoption of modern technology and scientific breeding, and low output limits farmer income, perpetuating the cycle — constraining the volume of quality milk available for procurement.

risks.risk: Livestock disease outbreaks and zoonotic threats
risks.note: Nipah Virus, Lumpy Skin Disease and Bovine Brucellosis are flagged as major threats to the dairy industry. Lingering effects of previous outbreaks combined with a fodder crisis have challenged industry growth, and structural issues such as lack of traceability for stray cattle make outbreaks difficult to prevent despite vaccination efforts; heightened public health warnings on raw unpasteurised milk also affect category perception.

risks.risk: Seasonality of milk production and price volatility
risks.note: Production peaks in the cooler flush season (September-February) and drops in the lean season (March-August), affecting production costs and availability. Processors manage supply by converting surplus flush-season milk into Skimmed Milk Powder to meet lean-season demand, which causes price volatility and supply imbalances — and exposes inventory positions across the year.

risks.risk: Competitive and market-price pressure, including from global dairy entrants
risks.note: Fluctuating market prices and the absence of a minimum support price make dairy farming less viable for small farmers. The entry of global dairy giants with aggressive pricing and economies of scale is a threat to local producers, and potential trade deals with countries such as the EU could restrict India's ability to control dairy exports and protect the domestic market. Separately, the shift to organised dairy is itself increasing competition among organised players.

Rising temperatures and erratic rainfall patterns can disrupt fodder production, increase feed costs and reduce milk yield. Management also names fluctuating weather conditions among the 'unforeseen external negativities' the workforce must help mitigate, and the BRSR identifies GHG emissions as a material risk on the basis that emissions will rise as manufacturing capacity grows with production demand.

Inadequate infrastructure including cold storage facilities and transportation networks can lead to milk spoilage and inefficient distribution, and lack of access to technology and information hinders adoption of efficient dairy farming practices. In addition, a segment of the population may not prioritise milk quality, limiting willingness to pay for higher-quality products — a constraint on premiumisation.

one-line thesis: Hatsun is on track to hit ₹10,000 Cr revenue run rate in FY26, driven by volume growth and proprietary distribution, but faces near-term margin pressure from 8-10% milk procurement hikes and 30-40% packaging cost inflation due to geopolitical supply chain disruptions.

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: Hatsun Agro Product Limited is the largest private sector dairy in India, manufacturing and marketing milk and value-added dairy products and ice creams from 22 plants across southern India, Maharashtra and Odisha.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: HAP manufactures and markets dairy products, especially milk and milk products such as curd, ghee, paneer and SMP, along with ice creams. It procures milk daily from over 500,000 farmers across most of the southern states of India and Maharashtra, chilled through Active Bulk Coolers at more than 1,553 locations, and sells directly, through distributors and through online platforms to end consumers. Milk and milk products account for 100% of turnover, with exports contributing 0.27% of total turnover.

BRSR Section A item 23 accordingly reports 'Nil' holding/subsidiary/associate companies/joint ventures at year end, and the Board's Report states the Company does not have any other subsidiary, joint venture or associate company.

segment_detail.title: Segment / subsidiary detail

products.title: Products & brands
products.body:
- **Fresh Dairy:** Arokya, Hatsun, HAP daily, Milky Moo, Arokya Standardised Milk, Arokya Full Cream Milk, Arokya Toned Milk, Arokya Double Toned Milk, Arokya Curd, Arokya Paneer, curd, ghee, cooking butter, table butter, lassi, buttermilk, paneer, yoghurt shakes, cheese spread, fresh cream

growth_optionality.body: Geographic expansion beyond Tamil Nadu (45% now, 50% target in 2 years); Formalization of unorganized dairy sector as tailwind; Own polythene film production mitigates some packaging risk

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Indian real GDP growth placed at 7.4 per cent in the First Advance Estimates for FY26, driven by domestic demand, with private consumption and capital formation supporting expansion; the FY27 outlook is shaped by these domestic strengths alongside evolving external conditions
- The dairy processing sector in India has a favourable outlook driven by rising disposable incomes, changing consumption patterns and increasing demand for healthy food supplements
- Structural shift from loose to branded, packaged and high-protein dairy, accelerating formalisation of the sector and increasing competition among organised players
- Urbanisation — India expected to have nearly 600 million urban residents by 2030, with urban households preferring branded and packaged milk, organised retail and e-commerce, and hygiene/quality/convenience
- Rising protein awareness, with ICMR recommending 0.83 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight, driving demand for protein-enriched milk, high-protein yogurt and lassi, and functional dairy beverages
- Branded dairy products growing 4-5 times faster than liquid milk in India, driven by innovation, convenience and higher margins, and linked to expansion of food service chains, QSRs and home consumption in Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities
- Quick commerce redefining dairy accessibility with 10-15 minute delivery, increasing demand for premium and branded dairy, expanding consumption into Tier-2 cities and encouraging impulse purchases
- India's ice cream market estimated at approximately USD 3.07 billion in 2026, projected to reach USD 5.39 billion by 2032 at a CAGR of around 9.84%, with volume growing at around 8.22% CAGR; impulse ice cream around 60.59% of 2026 market revenue and plant-based the fastest-growing category at around 14.19% volume CAGR
- Government support strengthening dairy infrastructure and productivity — NPDD, AHIDF, Rashtriya Gokul Mission and LHDC, plus the Kisan Credit Card ceiling raised to ₹5 lakh for agriculture and allied activities including dairy
- Union Budget 2026-27 raised the animal husbandry allocation to ₹6,153.46 Crores, a 16% increase over FY 2025-26 (₹5,302.83 Crores), with ₹1,055 Crores for NPDD, ₹2,010 Crores for LHDC, ₹800 Crores for Rashtriya Gokul Mission and ₹465 Crores for AHIDF
- Milk production growing at an accelerated 5%-6.5% pace, with high-pedigree cows expected to drive volume, while tighter regulatory standards and operational costs drive consolidation favouring organised, large-scale dairy processors
- Product-formulation trends towards lactose-free milk, probiotic yogurts, protein-fortified drinks, D2C subscription models, IoT/AI-enabled dairy-tech, and sustainable packaging

Inorganic expansion came through the acquisition of the Milky Moo brand via the shareholding of Milk Mantra Dairy Private Limited, adding processing facilities, a farmer network and a value-added product portfolio in the eastern markets; Milk Mantra Dairy Private Limited was subsequently amalgamated into Hatsun Agro Product Limited with an appointed date of 1st April 2025, sanctioned by the NCLT Cuttack Bench by order dated 10th March 2026. Retail expansion took the HAP daily network to 4,200+ outlets, extending beyond the traditional Tamil Nadu, Pondicherry, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana base into Maharashtra, Kerala, Odisha, Goa, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, West Bengal, Jharkhand, Gujarat, Bihar and the Andaman & Nicobar Islands; HAP daily also introduced Village Hubs taking reach deeper into rural markets, growing to over 169+ stores as of 31st March. On the ice cream side, a strong focus on expansion led to the opening of 54 IPlus outlets so far, while ibaco operated over 229 outlets as of 31st March. management_tone.body: Confident on volume growth and distribution advantage; Cautious on input cost inflation; Transparent about supply chain vulnerabilities; No guidance on FY27 profitability, only revenue trajectory

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Largest private sector dairy in India, with scale economies management says allow investment in production and distribution infrastructure 'affordable only by bigger Companies like us'
- Backward-integrated procurement: milk sourced daily from over 500,000 farmers, with over 13,226+ milk collection centre points and Active Bulk Coolers at more than 1,553 locations chilling milk within two hours
- Direct farmer relationship — payments made every 10 days directly into farmer bank accounts on Fat and SNF test results, supported by a dedicated database, plus artificial insemination and cattle-care services that improve yield and genetics
- Dense last-mile retail network: 4,200+ HAP daily outlets, 229+ ibaco outlets and 169+ HAP daily Village Hub stores as of 31st March 2026
- Multi-brand portfolio spanning fresh dairy (Arokya, Hatsun, Milky Moo), ice cream (Arun, ibaco), confectionery (Havia, Hanobar, Dako), beverages (Aniva) and cattle feed (Santosa)
- Brand trust built on quality control — Arokya milk undergoes 45 quality checks daily, well beyond the 32 mandatory tests prescribed by FSSAI; Arokya has over 30 years of presence since 1995
- Geographically distributed manufacturing: 22 plants across Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka, Maharashtra and Odisha, enabling efficient procurement and distribution
- Credit quality: CRISIL upgraded the long-term rating to CRISIL AA/Stable on 14th January 2026 from CRISIL AA-/Stable
- SAP ERP implementation supporting centralised online MIS control of operations across all units

themes.title: Consumption revival & FMCG premiumization
themes.need: Rural recovery, GST 2.0 and premiumization still frame the theme, but Q1FY27 rewarded portfolio SHAPE over volume. TATACONSUM's growth businesses hit INR 1,300cr (+47%) and are now 36% of India - larger than either salt (>INR 1,000cr) or tea & coffee (INR 1,200cr), with Sampann +58%, RTD +41% and Capital Foods INR 232cr (+40%) - while India tea revenue fell 4% on +2% volume as lower tea costs were deliberately passed back (tea inflation is now running 7-10% with most buying still ahead, so that inverts next year). PGHH shows the margin route: FY26 sales roughly flat at ~INR 4,300cr but PAT +19% to ~INR 850cr and ~100bps of structural margin from INR 86cr of productivity savings, absorbing crude and resin each up 30-50% with no stock-outs. The cautionary tale is licensed brands - JYOTHYLAB lost the Pril and Fa licences when Henkel did not renew (all manufacturing and selling stopped 1-June; Pril was ~7-8% of revenue, ~INR 225-240cr) and has filed SIAC arbitration. MARICO/DABUR/GODREJCP/COLPAL/EMAMILTD ride distribution + premium mix; VBL on beverage route-to-market; BIKAJI/GOPAL/BECTORFOOD on branded snacks; ORKLAINDIA took a 4% blended price increase in Q4 plus premium mix to a 16.9% EBITDA margin.
themes.driver: GST 2.0 demand pull-through; rural volume recovery; festive/wedding restocking; commodity pass-back timing; JYOTHYLAB's ~7-8% revenue hole and the SIAC arbitration.

themes.title: Agri value-chain - food processing, dairy, protein & seeds
themes.need: Rising protein/processed-food consumption, animal-nutrition demand and export tailwinds drive an integrated agri value-chain - DODLA/PARAGMILK on dairy; AVANTIFEED/SHINDL/SKMEGGPROD/HMAAGRO on aqua/poultry/meat protein; GODREJAGRO/KSCL/NATHBIOGEN on feed + seeds; REGAAL/SUKHJITS/GULPOLY on maize/starch; FOODSIN/MANORAMA on agri-processing & specialty fats.
themes.driver: Monsoon-led farm income; protein export demand; feed-margin recovery; festive processed-food restocking.
